questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presented with complaints of rhinorrhea, cough, and nasal congestion for 4 days. He was not experiencing severe headaches or problems with his vision. On physical exam, his vital signs were stable, and he was afebrile. He had some sinus tenderness to palpation but no periorbital edema present.
questions.lead_in: What would be the most appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation: Observation The patient has sinusitis. The most likely cause of this syndrome is a virus and would not warrant antibiotic therapy. The exception would be if the patient has an extended duration of symptoms (normally >7 days). The patient does not present with evidence of complications of sinusitis, such as severe headaches, visual disturbances, or neurologic deficits that would warrant ENT consultation or additional imaging. The best answer to the question would be just observation at this time.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q14

questions.question: A patient has an upper respiratory infection/sinusitis. A few weeks later they develop headache and low-grade fever. [image-based question: forehead abscess and a subdural abscess]
questions.question_raw: Patient upper resp infection/sinus. A few weeks later, headache, low grade fever.

parts.text: Name the syndrome and complication shown on the image (forehead abscess with subdural abscess).
Name the organism or group of organisms that is the most likely pathogen.

parts_raw.text: What is the name of the syndrome and complication (as seen on the image provided - picture of forehead abscess and a subdural abscess - Pott's puffy tumor)
What is the organism or group of organisms that is the most likely pathogen

questions.model_answer: a) Pott's puffy tumor - frontal sinusitis complicated by frontal bone osteomyelitis with a subperiosteal (forehead) abscess; the intracranial complication shown is a subdural empyema. b) Aerobic streptococci, particularly the Streptococcus anginosus (Streptococcus milleri) group, which dominate the flora of chronic sinusitis-associated intracranial suppuration (streptococci in 25%-45% of subdural empyema cases). c) (1) Staphylococci including Staphylococcus aureus (10%-15%). (2) Anaerobic streptococci. (3) Other anaerobes (e.g., anaerobic gram-negative bacilli). (4) Aerobic gram-negative bacilli (3%-10%); infections are frequently polymicrobial. d) Surgical drainage plus empiric IV antimicrobials directed at staphylococci, streptococci, aerobic gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes: vancomycin plus metronidazole plus a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin (e.g., ceftriaxone or cefepime), adjusted by Gram stain and culture; parenteral therapy for 3-4 weeks after drainage (longer with osteomyelitis).
questions.beyond_mandell: The eponym 'Pott's puffy tumor' is not used in this Mandell chapter; the entity (frontal osteomyelitis with subperiosteal abscess and associated subdural empyema) is established ID/neurosurgical knowledge.

questions.question: Preseptal versus orbital cellulitis and its complications.

parts.text: What is the anatomic structure that differentiates between preseptal and orbital cellulitis
Name 5 clinical signs/symptoms that would suggest orbital cellulitis over preseptal
Sinusitis of which sinus leads to highest risk for orbital cellulitis and why
Patient now has ipsilateral lateral nerve palsy. What complication are you worried about

parts_raw.text: What is the anatomic structure that differentiates between preseptal and orbital cellulitis (0.5)
Name 5 clinical signs/symptoms that would suggest orbital cellulitis over preseptal (2.5)
Sinusitis of which sinus leads to highest risk for orbital cellulitis and why (1)
Patient now has ipsilateral lateral nerve palsy. What complication are you worried about (0.5)

questions.model_answer:
a) The orbital septum — a thin fibrous membrane from the orbital periosteum at the rim to the tarsal plates; infection anterior to it is preseptal (lids only), posterior to it is orbital (fat and muscle within the bony orbit).
b) (1) Proptosis. (2) Ophthalmoplegia. (3) Pain on extraocular movement/deep eye pain. (4) Diplopia. (5) Decreased visual acuity with afferent pupillary defect (chemosis also supports orbital involvement).
c) The ethmoid sinus: its lateral wall is the paper-thin lamina papyracea, which forms the medial orbital wall, contains multiple foramina for nerves and vessels, and may have natural Zuckerkandl dehiscences — so infection readily crosses to collect beneath the medial periorbita. Ethmoid sinusitis is the most common cause of sinus-related orbital infection and causes nearly all subperiosteal abscesses.
d) Septic cavernous sinus thrombophlebitis — suspect it with CN VI palsy, contralateral orbital signs within 24-48 hours, or bilateral CN III/IV/VI neuropathies ± V1/V2 sensory loss; image with MRI/MRV.

cohort_answer.text: Anatomic structure: Orbital septum - thin fibrous membrane serving as barrier between superficial lids and orbit; infections anterior to septum are preseptal, posterior are orbital (Mandell's); preseptal involves only lids not the orbit, orbital cellulitis involves soft tissues (fat, muscle) within bony orbit. Signs of orbital cellulitis: Proptosis; Painful extraocular eye movement; Ophthalmoplegia; Diplopia; Chemosis. Highest risk sinus: Ethmoid - separated from orbit by thin lamina papyracea (medial wall of orbit), contains multiple foramina for nerves/vessels, some people have natural defects; nearly all periosteal abscesses secondary to ethmoid sinusitis. Complication to rule out with cranial nerve palsy: Cavernous sinus thrombosis - spread to opposite eye through cavernous sinus usually within 24-48 hours of initial unilateral orbital findings; may present with bilateral findings or signs of bilateral neuropathies of CN III, IV, VI without lid edema/erythema typical of orbital cellulitis, especially from skin infections of middle third of face or dental infections
